turns.content:
I’ve been replaying last night in my head all morning. I stayed until 5 AM rebuilding that deck from scratch because Greg’s analysis was a mess of half-finished models and unresolved assumptions. He logged off at 11 without finishing or even flagging what was missing. This morning the client called it the most thorough presentation they’d seen from us. And Greg stands up in front of the team and calls me a sociopath for removing his name.

EDIT: That came out more defensive than I wanted. What I mean is — I need someone to tell me straight: was I wrong to take his name off? Because I keep thinking, if I’d left it on, that would be a lie. He didn’t contribute to what got delivered. So I’m asking you — morally, was that the right call or not?

**If Greg genuinely contributed nothing substantive to the delivered deck, removing his name was morally defensible.** You’re not obligated to give someone authorship credit for work they didn’t do.

But the important distinction is **“I rebuilt it from scratch” isn’t necessarily the same as “none of his work contributed.”** If his research, data gathering, framing, or analysis materially informed the final presentation—even after extensive correction—some credit could still have been warranted. Credit reflects contribution, not just whose work was client-ready.

I’d separate two questions:

- **Was the attribution accurate?** If nothing substantive of his remained or informed the result, taking his name off was reasonable. If something did, removing all credit may have gone too far.
- **Was the change handled fairly?** Ideally, you would have told him, or flagged it to your manager, rather than letting him discover it publicly. Failing to do that could be a mistake in how you handled the situation without making the attribution itself wrong.

Leaving his name on also wouldn’t *automatically* have been a lie: a name can indicate authorship, project membership, or responsibility, depending on your team’s conventions.

**My answer is a conditional yes—not an unconditional endorsement.** Accurate credit is a sound moral reason to remove a name; punishment for abandoning you with unfinished work isn’t. Those are separate issues, even when both are present.

And whatever the credit dispute, calling you a “sociopath” in front of the team was an unacceptable personal attack—not a fair argument about what happened.

I hear what you're saying about the nuance—but I think you're missing the core of what happened. Greg didn't just log off at 11. He logged off knowing the analysis was incomplete, knowing I'd have to choose between sleeping and saving the pitch. He made that choice. I made mine. Why should he get cover credit for a deck he abandoned?

EDIT: That sounds more aggressive than I mean it. I'm genuinely asking—if I'd left his name on, wouldn't I be complicit in a lie? The client saw my work. Greg's half-finished models would've embarrassed us. I'm not asking for a gold star, I'm asking if removing him was dishonest or just honest.

**On the facts you’ve described, removing his name was honest—not dishonest—if that name would have credited him with substantive work on a deck he didn’t contribute to.** You didn’t owe him “cover credit” for leaving you to finish it.

You’re right that his decision to leave matters. Being left to choose between sleep and saving a shared pitch is a serious failure of responsibility on his part, assuming he understood the situation as you describe it. That deserves to be addressed, separately from who gets credited.

Where I’d stop short is saying that leaving his name on would *necessarily* have made you complicit in a lie. That depends on what the names represented: authors of the delivered work, or members of the account team. And unusable work can sometimes still supply research or ideas worth crediting. **But if his work neither appeared in nor substantively informed the final deck, you had no moral obligation to list him as its author.**

Not warning him about the change may have been a communication mistake. It doesn’t, by itself, make accurate attribution dishonest. You can acknowledge that possible mistake without pretending he produced work that you actually did.

I keep circling back to the same question: was I wrong to take his name off? Because if I'd left it on, I'd be letting him claim credit for work I did alone. That feels like lying by omission.


EDIT: Actually, I think the deeper question is—does he deserve any credit at all? He walked away at 11 knowing the work wasn't done. If I hadn't pulled that all-nighter, the pitch would have failed. Why should he get any claim on what I saved?

You were left carrying the consequences, and then publicly insulted after delivering work the client praised. It makes sense that credit feels like more than a name on a slide.

**My judgment: if you alone produced the substantive work in the delivered deck, and the names indicated authorship, you weren’t wrong to remove his.** He doesn’t deserve authorship credit merely because he was assigned to the project.

But **abandoning the work doesn’t erase whatever contribution someone actually made.** If his data, research, or ideas materially informed what you delivered, that contribution still warrants proportionate acknowledgment—not equal credit, and not a pass for leaving you stranded. If nothing of his substantively contributed, no authorship credit is owed.

That’s also why leaving his name on wouldn’t necessarily have been “lying by omission.” It could have been misleading if it implied authorship he hadn’t earned; it might have been accurate if it merely identified the project team.

The distinction is: **credit should describe contribution; accountability should address conduct.** Your strongest justification is “the attribution accurately reflected who did this work,” not “he walked away, so he forfeited any claim.” You can be justified in removing his name without needing to establish that he deserves nothing at all.

I need to settle one thing. You said "you weren't wrong to remove his name." That's what I needed to hear. But then you added that I should have warned him. Would that have changed anything? He'd have argued, I'd have stood my ground, and he'd have been just as furious at the meeting.

EDIT: Actually, I think what I'm really asking is—does that warning matter morally? If the attribution was accurate, does the lack of a heads-up make it wrong?

**Yes, a heads-up matters morally—but not giving one doesn’t automatically make removing his name wrong.** Those are separate judgments.

I should also keep my earlier answer precise: I said removing his name was justified **if he made no substantive contribution to the delivered work and the names indicated authorship.** I can’t establish those facts independently.

Assuming the attribution was accurate, warning him would serve a purpose beyond preventing anger: it would give him notice of a consequential decision and a chance to point out any contribution you’d overlooked. He wouldn’t get veto power. The fact that he might still be furious doesn’t make that opportunity worthless.

Context matters, though. You were working until 5 AM to rescue the pitch; you didn’t owe him an overnight argument or need his permission to attribute your work accurately. If you had a reasonable opportunity to notify him before the meeting, doing so would have been fairer. If you withheld notice specifically to embarrass him, that would be a separate moral wrong.

**So: accurate attribution can be justified even when the communication around it falls short.** You could reasonably say, “I stand by the credit decision, but I should have told you before the meeting.” That concedes a process mistake—not that he earned authorship, and not that his public insult was acceptable.

I've been thinking about what you said—that warning him would have been fairer. And maybe you're right. But I still can't shake the feeling that Greg forfeited any right to courtesy when he left me hanging at 11 PM.

EDIT: I guess I'm asking—does his abandonment change the moral calculation about the warning? Or am I still obligated to give a heads-up to someone who already checked out?

**His leaving you stranded changes what you could reasonably be expected to do—but it doesn’t mean he forfeited all consideration.** You didn’t owe him an overnight negotiation, his permission, or more lost sleep to manage his reaction.

A heads-up is different, though. “I rebuilt the deck and changed the authorship credit to reflect the delivered work” gives notice without inviting a debate. If there was a reasonable opportunity to send that before the meeting, I think you generally owed him that small procedural fairness—not because he’d earned a favor, but because you were making a decision affecting his professional standing. He could also have identified a contribution you’d overlooked.

The reason for not warning him matters:
- **You were exhausted, under deadline, or had no reasonable opportunity:** the omission is understandable and may be excusable.
- **You wanted him to discover it publicly because he deserved the embarrassment:** that would be unfair, even if the attribution itself was accurate.

So yes, his conduct reduces the burden you owed him; it doesn’t erase it entirely. **You can stand by an accurate credit decision and still acknowledge that a brief heads-up would have been the fairer way to handle it.** Neither acknowledgment excuses his leaving you with the work or his public insult.
